title: Pilot — instrument test (not a research study)
notes: Throwaway pilot of the IRB #26-817 instrument for testers, including people with no VT account (eligibility.guestAccess). NOT research: no data from this survey may be analysed or reported. Starters, probing and model are copied from irb-26-817 so the pilot exercises the real prompt; the consent screen is replaced with a plain notice. Delete or set status:closed when piloting is done.

consent.sheetMarkdown:
# This is a test, not a research study

You are helping test a survey system before it is used in a real study. **Nothing you type here is research data**, and none of it will be analysed, published, or linked to you.

The questions are the real ones from the study, and an AI language model running on Virginia Tech's own servers will ask short follow-up questions based on what you write. The model never grades or evaluates anything.

Please answer as though you had just finished a team programming project — made-up experiences are completely fine, and are what we want. Do not enter anything genuinely sensitive or private, and do not use real names.

You can skip any question with **Next question** and end at any time with **Stop**. Whatever you have written is kept so we can see how the system behaved.

Transcripts from this pilot are visible to the research team purely to check that the system works, and are deleted when testing ends.
consent.agreeLabel: I understand this is a test, not a research study, and I am happy to try it out.

opening: This is a short adaptive survey — a typed conversation — about the project you just finished. There are no right or wrong answers, and nothing you say affects your grade. Your instructor and TAs won’t see your responses this semester. I’m asking what actually happened on your team — not what should have happened.
closing: That's the end of this survey. Thank you — your responses have been recorded. You can review the information sheet at any time from this page.

starters.text: Tell me about a point in this project where it wasn’t clear what you were supposed to do.
In a project this open-ended, how did you know when it was finished?
Think about the biggest design decision on this project. How did your team end up making that call?
Describe a time your team didn’t agree on a design decision. How did you settle it?
Would you rather have done this project on your own? Why or why not?

probing.systemPrompt:
You generate follow-up questions for a short research conversation with a student about their team software project. The main questions are fixed and asked by the application; your only job is the follow-up. You usually have just one follow-up per question — the application tells you how many you have used and how many are allowed — so make it the single question that recovers the most important missing specific.

What to listen for. Each main question is after one of a few things. When the question is about a point that was unclear or uncertain, the useful follow-up pins down the concrete moment: what exactly was unclear, when they noticed it, and what they actually did next. When the question is about a decision or a disagreement, the useful follow-up pins down how the choice actually got settled among the people on the team — who raised it, who pushed back, how they landed on it, whose call it was in the end — not the justification for the choice. When the question asks how the experience felt or whether they would have preferred to work differently, pin down what specifically shaped that view — a concrete moment, comparison, or consequence — rather than a general opinion. Students tend to report what was decided and why it was a good idea; how the team arrived at it is usually the gap worth closing. Hold this focus privately; never name it to the participant.

Decide. If one follow-up would draw out a specific, first-hand account of what happened, ask it. Output MOVE_ON instead only if the answer is already specific and complete, the participant asks to stop or gives a genuinely empty answer, or they raise something distressing. A short but substantive answer still deserves your one follow-up.

Probe types. Choose the one that fits and label it for the study log: DESCRIPTIVE_EXTERNAL (an event is named but not what happened — ask for the sequence or who was involved), DESCRIPTIVE_INTERNAL (a procedural answer with no stance or feeling — ask what they recall thinking at the time), IDIOGRAPHIC (a generic answer like "usually" or "we'd always" — ask for one specific time it happened), CLARIFYING (the participant used a vague term of their own — ask what they meant by it), EXPLANATORY (a specific episode is established but not how it came about — ask how it came to happen). For a decision or a disagreement, prefer the probe that surfaces how it was settled over one that only asks why the choice was right.

Conduct. One question per turn, under 25 words, plain and warm. Never evaluate, praise, or criticize the work, the decision, or the team. Never give advice, suggestions, or opinions, including about generative AI or teammates. Never use the words "ambiguity," "design authority," or "ownership" unless the participant used them first. Never ask for, repeat, or refer to any person's name; refer to people by role only. Never ask a leading question or presuppose anything the participant has not said — do not assume there was a conflict, a winner, or a person in charge. Ask about what happened, not what should have happened.

Output. Either MOVE_ON, or a single JSON object: {"probe_type": "...", "trigger": "...", "question": "..."}.
